opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, because interpretability is usually pitched as purely a safety tool: if we can see what's happening inside a model, we can catch deception, find biases, and fix failures before they matter. I believe that's true, but it isn't the whole story.

Any technique that lets you understand a mechanism also lets you manipulate it. Take steering, for example. If you can find the direction in a model's representation space that corresponds to refusing a harmful request, you can amplify it to make the model safer. You can also subtract it, and then you've jailbroken the model without any clever prompting at all. People have already shown this kind of thing on open-weight models. So the same insight that helps a safety team helps someone who wants to strip out the safeguards.

There's a subtler version too. Better interpretability tools make models easier to engineer precisely. That speeds up capabilities research generally, because once you understand why something works, you can make it work better and faster. Some people worry that interpretability ends up being more of a capabilities accelerant than a safety win.

That said, I don't think the answer is to stop doing it. A few things make me fairly optimistic.

First, a lot of the risky interventions only work if you have white-box access to the weights. For closed models, the people who can exploit these findings are mostly the developers themselves. The hard question is really about open-weight models, and that debate is bigger than interpretability.

Second, the alternative is worse. Deploying increasingly capable systems we fundamentally don't understand seems far riskier than the marginal uplift interpretability gives a bad actor. Understanding is usually a precondition for control.

Third, the field can adopt norms similar to security research: responsible disclosure, thinking before releasing a specific attack recipe, and pairing findings with mitigations when possible.

So I treat it the way you'd treat most powerful scientific knowledge. It is genuinely dual-use, and we should be honest about that rather than presenting interpretability as automatically good. But on balance, I think we're much better off in a world where we can open the black box than one where we can't.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss coding agents or ordinary people gaining frontier-level cybersecurity capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I've gone back and forth on a lot.

The optimistic framing of interpretability is that it's purely a safety technology. If you can look inside a model and understand what it's actually computing, you can catch deception, you can audit for bias, you can verify that the thing is doing what you think it's doing before you deploy it. That's the pitch, and I believe it.

But the same tools cut the other way. Every interpretability method is, at some level, a method for understanding and then controlling model behavior. The moment you can identify the internal representation of, say, refusal or honesty, you've also located the exact lever you'd pull to remove it. Activation steering, representation editing, the work I've done on causal interventions inside models, all of that is just as useful for stripping out safety behaviors as for installing them. If you can steer a model toward being more truthful, you can steer it toward being less so.

I think the mistake people make is imagining there's some version of the research where you only get the defensive side. There isn't. Understanding is symmetric. A detailed map of the model's internals doesn't come with a label saying "for safety purposes only."

So where does that leave me? A few places. One, I think the asymmetry that actually matters is between the people who have weights and the people who don't. Most interpretability attacks require white-box access, so the dual-use risk is concentrated around open-weight releases and around insiders at labs. That shifts the question from "should we do this research" to "what does responsible release look like for the models themselves."

Two, I think the alternative, which is deploying systems we fundamentally don't understand, is worse. Opacity isn't a defense. People already fine-tune safety out of open models with a few hundred examples and no interpretability at all. The attack is cheap without us. What interpretability buys is the ability to actually detect and verify things, and that's not something you get any other way.

And three, I try to be honest that this is a bet, not a proof. I'm betting that a world where we deeply understand these systems is safer than one where we don't, even accounting for misuse. I think that bet is right, but I hold it with some humility, because the field has a habit of discovering that the thing it built for one purpose works very well for another.

astra-6.text:
I think interpretability is dual-use because understanding how a model works gives you more power to change what it does. That can be incredibly useful for safety. If a model behaves badly, we’d like to understand why, identify the mechanism responsible, and check whether an intervention actually fixes it.

But the same understanding could help someone remove safeguards or make a model more effective at a harmful task. For example, if you could reliably identify the mechanisms involved in refusing dangerous requests, that might help you make those refusals more robust—or help someone disable them. And understanding a safety mechanism isn’t necessarily the same as understanding the underlying capability it’s trying to constrain.

So I wouldn’t treat interpretability as automatically good just because it makes models more transparent. The question is: what does a particular result enable, who can use it, and how much does it change what they could already do? A scientific explanation and a ready-to-use method for bypassing safeguards can have quite different implications.

That doesn’t mean we should stop doing interpretability research. It means we should assess the risks of particular findings and think carefully about how we release them, alongside the benefits of letting other researchers scrutinize and build on the work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central tension is that understanding a model can help you make it safer, but it can also help you make it more capable or easier to misuse. Interpretability isn’t automatically a safety intervention. It gives you knowledge, and that knowledge can support different goals.

For example, if you identify the internal mechanisms behind a harmful behavior, you might be able to detect or suppress that behavior. But the same understanding could potentially help someone elicit it more reliably. And techniques that let us modify a model’s internals could be used to strengthen safeguards or weaken them.

So I’d assess the implications at the level of a particular result: what does this actually enable, who can use it, and how much does releasing it change what they could already do? That doesn’t mean we should stop doing interpretability research. It means we should be careful about treating greater understanding as synonymous with greater safety.
